Communication-Efficient LLM Adaptation over Decentralized GPU Meshes

Sameera Ramasinghe Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Shamane Siriwardhana Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Hadi Mohaghegh Dolatabadi Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Chamin P Hewa Koneputugodage Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Gil Avraham Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Violetta Shevchenko Affiliation: Pluralis Research    James Snewin Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Karol Pajak Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Harry Xi Affiliation: Pluralis Research    Alexander Long Affiliation: Pluralis Research
Abstract

Decentralized training enables large-model training over low-end GPUs and internet-grade connections, but communication along both data-parallel and pipeline-parallel axes becomes the primary bottleneck. We study post-pretraining adaptation in this setting. We propose an asynchronous two-circuit system: a fast compressed training circuit drives throughput using activation masking for pipeline-parallel (PP) transfer and compressed data-parallel (DP) synchronization, while a slow anchor circuit runs occasional unmasked forward–backward passes off the critical path. Then, we introduce a spectral correction optimizer that uses these delayed anchor priors to denoise masked gradients without blocking the fast stream. Although prior work has found aggressive activation compression unreliable, we show that masking supports post-pretraining adaptation at high compression rates when anchored this way. Pipeline-parallel compression alone yields up to a 9×9\times throughput gain, and combining it with data-parallel compression increases beyond 40×40\times over internet-grade ∼200\sim 200Mbps connections, while matching dense uncompressed performance across domain adaptation and continual pretraining.

1 Introduction

Training and adapting frontier models typically requires tightly connected datacenter clusters, putting modern AI research out of reach for smaller labs, independent researchers, and open communities (Narayanan et al., 2021; Grattafiori et al., 2024). Decentralized training offers an alternative: computation can be distributed over the Internet across heterogeneous consumer-grade GPUs, allowing participants to contribute otherwise fragmented compute (Diskin et al., 2021; Ryabinin et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2022; Douillard et al., 2023; Jaghouar et al., 2024; Ajanthan et al., 2026; Ramasinghe et al., 2025c). We focus on decentralized post-pretraining adaptation, i.e., fine-tuning or continual pretraining open-weight models over such GPU meshes.

This setting is fundamentally communication-limited. Commodity Internet links provide bandwidth on the order of hundreds of Mbps, compared to hundreds of Gbps in datacenter interconnects. A practical system must therefore reduce communication along both distributed-training axes: data parallelism (DP), where replicas synchronize weight gradients, and pipeline parallelism (PP), where model shards exchange activations and activation gradients.

DP communication can be reduced with gradient compression (Vogels et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2024) or sparse synchronization (Douillard et al., 2023; Douillard et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2024; Jaghouar et al., 2024; Sani et al., 2024), but these methods still assume that each worker or replica group can host a full model. PP addresses the complementary regime: it enables models that do not fit on a single low-end GPU by partitioning them across layers. However, PP compression is substantially more delicate. Standard compression methods such as sparsification, quantization, and low-rank projection often degrade performance at high compression rates due to error accumulation across layers (Rudakov et al., 2023; Ramasinghe et al., 2025b). Recent methods such as Subspace Networks (Ramasinghe et al., 2025b) and Pufferfish (Wang et al., 2021) mitigate this during pretraining by imposing structural constraints, but these constraints make them difficult to apply to arbitrary pretrained checkpoints.

We therefore revisit and refine a simple but previously discarded idea: activation masking. Our key observation is that adaptation differs from pretraining. During post-pretraining adaptation, weights evolve slowly from a strong pretrained initialization, and the goal is often to find a useful update direction rather than learn representations from scratch. In contrast to the pessimistic view in prior works (Ramasinghe et al., 2025b; Rudakov et al., 2023), we show that sparse activation signals are sufficient for the main training stream, provided they are anchored by higher-fidelity information. We realize this idea with a two-circuit decentralized system. A fast compressed circuit performs most updates using in-graph activation masking along the PP axis and compressed synchronization along the DP axis. In parallel, a slower anchor circuit occasionally runs full unmasked forward and backward passes. These unmasked passes do not block the fast circuit; instead, their gradients arrive asynchronously as Anchor Priors, which denoise and steer the masked optimization trajectory. The asynchrony is principled: fine-tuning gradients live in a low-dimensional (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Gur-Ari et al., 2018), slowly-drifting subspace, so a stale unmasked gradient still points roughly the right way (Neyshabur et al., 2020; Wortsman et al., 2022). This is akin to the same structural property that makes model merging effective (Wortsman et al., 2022), applied here at the gradient level.

To use these delayed priors effectively, we introduce a spectral correction optimizer. It maintains a slow-moving momentum buffer over anchor gradients and uses its principal directions to reweight masked updates: anchor-supported eigendirections are reinforced, while unsupported noisy directions are damped. We complement this design with a convergence analysis identifying when the correction provably helps: when fine-tuning gradients lie in a low-dimensional subspace and the optimization trajectory drifts slowly, the anchor basis remains informative despite staleness. The analysis also clarifies why random PRF masking is essential; it produces an approximately unbiased gradient estimator that the spectral filter can denoise, while top-KK masking introduces a structured bias the filter cannot remove. Empirically, the system is robust to substantial staleness, and significantly superior to top-KK, reinforcing these predictions.

Across domain adaptation, continual pretraining, and reasoning-oriented training, our method matches or exceeds dense uncompressed training while substantially improving throughput over low-bandwidth links. PP compression alone yields up to a 9×9\times throughput gain, and combining it with DP compression increases this over 40×40\times. The method generalizes across model families, depths, widths, and mesh sizes, and produces models that are more robust to pruning. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose a two-circuit decentralized training system in which a fast masked circuit trains continuously while a slower unmasked anchor circuit asynchronously supplies high-fidelity gradient priors, decoupling throughput from the cost of clean gradient signals.

  • •

    We introduce a spectral correction optimizer that uses delayed Anchor Priors to denoise masked gradients. Our convergence analysis and empirical results demonstrate its efficacy.

  • •

    We show superior performance among competing methods, matching uncompressed adaptation while achieving over a 40×40\times throughput. Further, models trained with our method are more robust to pruning, improving their suitability for resource-constrained inference.

2 Related Works

Data parallel compression.

Decentralized DP training has motivated two lines of work: 1) Sparse synchronization methods reduce the number of all-reduces by performing many local optimizer steps between outer updates (Douillard et al., 2023; Douillard et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2024; Jaghouar et al., 2024; Sani et al., 2024); we use Streaming DiLoCo (Douillard et al., 2025), which overlaps the outer synchronization with local computation. 2) Low-rank gradient compressors reduce communication volume by transmitting low-rank approximations of the gradient (Vogels et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2024); we combine PowerSGD (Vogels et al., 2019) with Streaming DiLoCo. However, the proposed design can be integrated with other DP alternatives. Pipeline-parallel activation compression. Quantization-based methods cast activations and activation gradients to lower-precision formats with error compensation: AQ-SGD (Wang et al., 2022) compresses activation changes between epochs to enable error feedback over slow networks, and TAH-Quant (He et al., 2025) extends this with tile-wise adaptive Hadamard quantization. These methods operate off-graph, transmitting compressed payloads that are decompressed before use, which decouples forward and backward sparsity patterns and requires storing per-example state across epochs to support error feedback. We instead use in-graph random masking with no error feedback. Our masking is also substantially more aggressive (95%95\% vs. 4×4\times/8×8\times quantization). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning. reduces training VRAM by using low-rank adapters (Hu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2024; Lialin et al., 2023; Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021), but the forward and backward passes still transmit full dense activations across pipeline-parallel boundaries. Thus, they do not address the communication bottleneck. Our method composes cleanly with PEFT (Section 6).

3 Methodology

We consider decentralized post-pretraining adaptation over a low-bandwidth GPU mesh across DP and PP dimensions. We represent a decentralized mesh as a 2D X×YX\times Y grid, where XX is the data-parallel (DP) dimension and YY is the pipeline-parallel (PP) dimension. Each worker stores only a subset of the model layers, and workers communicate over low-bandwidth links along both DP and PP axes. For all experiments, we partition the mesh into two asynchronous circuits: an (X−Z)×Y(X-Z)\times Y fast masked circuit and a Z×YZ\times Y unmasked anchor circuit. In all our experiments, we fix Z=1Z=1.

The anchor circuit occasionally runs unmasked forward–backward passes and supplies high-fidelity gradient signals that the fast circuit uses to denoise its compressed updates. The anchor circuit does not block the fast circuit: its gradients are consumed asynchronously when they arrive, so the fast circuit’s throughput is set by masked communication only. This split is the core design move. Activation masking alone reduces communication but introduces noise that compounds across boundaries; running unmasked passes synchronously would eliminate the throughput gain. Asynchronous anchors give us both, i.e., masked-step throughput, plus a slow correctional signal that does not enter the critical path.

3.1 Activation Masking for PP Compression

Let h∈ℝT×Hh\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H} denote the hidden-state tensor at a masked inter-layer boundary, where TT is sequence length and HH is hidden size. On masked steps we apply elementwise masking h~=h⊙m\tilde{h}=h\odot m with m∈{0,1}T×Hm\in\{0,1\}^{T\times H} at masking probability pp, retaining K=round⁡((1−p)​H)K=\mathrm{round}((1-p)H) dimensions per token.

Shared PRF avoids transmitting the mask.

Naively, masking would require sending the retained indices for every token alongside the values, halving the compression benefit. We avoid this by generating mm from a shared deterministic pseudorandom function M=g⁡(ℓ,t,B,S,H)M=g(\ell,t,B,S,H) keyed on layer index, optimization step, and batch metadata. Sender and receiver reconstruct the same mask locally; only the KK retained values are transmitted.

In-graph masking gives matched forward/backward sparsity.

Because masking is applied in-graph as a multiplication, the backward pass inherits the same pattern automatically: ∂ℒ/∂ht,j=(∂ℒ/∂h~t,j)​mt,j.\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h_{t,j}=(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\tilde{h}_{t,j})\,m_{t,j}. Any entry masked in the forward has exactly zero backward gradient, so the same retained positions can be reused for backward activation-gradient transmission. This gives the same compression rate in both directions and avoids the need to track separate forward and backward sparsity patterns. It also distinguishes our scheme from off-graph transport compression, where forward and backward compression are decoupled and can drift out of correspondence with the derivative of the executed computation (e.g., decoupled Top-KK or quantization). Note that We deliberately use random masking instead top-KK because 1) top-KK is biased by construction, and as we show, this bias propagates through the descent inequality as a non-vanishing floor, and 2) the spectral correction we introduce next contracts zero-mean isotropic noise but cannot remove a structured bias (see Appendix F for a full analysis).

3.2 Anchor Priors and Spectral Correction

Activation masking reduces PP communication but injects noise into every gradient. We need a denoising signal, but one that does not eliminate the throughput gains we just bought. Fine-tuning makes a useful option viable: gradients live in a slowly drifting low-dimensional subspace, so a stale unmasked gradient still carries useful information. We exploit this with an asynchronous anchor circuit that runs occasional unmasked passes and uses their geometry to denoise the fast masked gradients without blocking them.

Asynchronous anchor circuit.

A naive synchronous fix would periodically disable masking and run a full unmasked forward–backward pass through the main pipeline. At our target bandwidth this is prohibitively expensive: an unmasked pass sends roughly 1/(1−p)1/(1-p) more activation data per boundary, and the entire fast circuit waits while it runs (Appendix H). Our alternative is to spin off a parallel anchor circuit that runs unmasked passes from a slightly stale weight snapshot, asynchronously, and feeds its gradients back to the fast circuit when they arrive. The fast circuit never waits. The cost is that anchor gradients are delayed (we measure Δ≈20\Delta\approx 20–2525 fast-circuit steps in our configuration), so they cannot be used as exact gradient updates, i.e., they can only inform optimization geometry. This is the restriction that shapes the rest of the design.

A separate momentum buffer for unmasked gradients.

For each targeted weight matrix WW, we maintain an EMA of arriving anchor gradients,

Mtanc=βanc​Mt−anc+(1−βanc)​Gτanc,M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}=\beta_{\mathrm{anc}}M_{t^{-}}^{\mathrm{anc}}+(1-\beta_{\mathrm{anc}})G_{\tau}^{\mathrm{anc}}, (1)

where t−t^{-} is the optimizer state immediately before the anchor gradient arrives. Two design choices here. First, we keep this momentum separate from AdamW’s first moment mtm_{t} rather than folding anchor gradients into it: mtm_{t} is updated on every fast step and is dominated by masked-step noise, so blending stale unmasked gradients into it would either dilute their signal or, with an aggressive blend, introduce slow oscillations. A separate buffer lets us treat anchor gradients on their own terms. Second, we use an EMA rather than the latest anchor gradient because individual anchor gradients are themselves noisy stochastic estimates. We choose βanc\beta_{\mathrm{anc}} large enough to average over several anchor cycles, since the gradient subspace drifts slowly during fine-tuning (Section E.3).

From momentum to a denoising operator:

Given MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}, we want to extract the directions in parameter space that are repeatedly reinforced by unmasked gradients, i.e., the geometry the fast circuit’s noisy gradients should be pulled toward. Singular value decomposition is the natural choice: Mtanc=Ut​St​Vt⊤M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}=U_{t}S_{t}V_{t}^{\top} identifies left and right subspaces with strength quantified by the singular values sis_{i}. Directions with large sis_{i} are those the anchor circuit has consistently observed; directions with small sis_{i} are either weakly supported or absent. We use SVD rather than, e.g., Hessian eigendecomposition (which we cannot afford at scale) or AdamW’s second moment vtv_{t} (which is dominated by masked-step variance and reflects noise structure, not signal structure).

Filtering di=si/(si+τp)d_{i}=s_{i}/(s_{i}+\tau_{p}).

Given the anchor basis (Ut,Vt)(U_{t},V_{t}), we need to decide how to use it. Hard projection onto the top-rr singular subspace is one option but requires choosing rr, and discards information about how strongly each direction is supported. Instead, we apply a soft filter

di=sisi+τp,d_{i}=\frac{s_{i}}{s_{i}+\tau_{p}}, (2)

which has three useful properties. First, it is bounded between 00 and 11, so the filter never amplifies the gradient. Second, it is adaptive: directions with si≫τps_{i}\gg\tau_{p} pass nearly unattenuated (di→1d_{i}\to 1), while directions with si≪τps_{i}\ll\tau_{p} are damped (di→0d_{i}\to 0). Third, it requires only one hyperparameter τp\tau_{p}, which sets the scale of "weakly supported," rather than a hard rank cutoff. The form s/(s+τp)s/(s+\tau_{p}) is the standard Tikhonov-regularized soft threshold, familiar from inverse problems, and gives a Lipschitz filter that is well-behaved as the anchor momentum evolves.

Two-sided application.

For a matrix gradient GtmaskG_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}, we transform into the anchor basis, Xt=Ut⊤​Gtmask​Vt,X_{t}=U_{t}^{\top}G_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}V_{t}, apply the filter to both index axes, Xtfilt=diag⁡(d)​Xt​diag​(d),X_{t}^{\mathrm{filt}}=\mathrm{diag}(d)X_{t}\mathrm{diag}(d), and reconstruct Gtfilt=Ut​Xtfilt​Vt⊤.G_{t}^{\mathrm{filt}}=U_{t}X_{t}^{\mathrm{filt}}V_{t}^{\top}. Two-sided filtering reflects that for a matrix-valued gradient, both the row space (which input features are active) and the column space (which output features are active) carry information. The anchor circuit observes both; restricting to one side discards half the geometric information.

The final gradient passed to AdamW is

Gtproj=α​Gtmask+(1−α)​Gtfilt.G_{t}^{\mathrm{proj}}=\alpha G_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}+(1-\alpha)G_{t}^{\mathrm{filt}}. (3)

We do not use the filtered gradient alone. The reason is that the anchor basis is an EMA of stale gradients, so GtfiltG_{t}^{\mathrm{filt}} inherits some staleness; the masked gradient is noisy but reflects the current weights. Blending preserves the current-iterate information while pulling toward the anchor’s reliable subspace. The blend coefficient α\alpha trades these off: α=1\alpha=1 recovers masked-only training (no denoising), α=0\alpha=0 uses only the filtered gradient (maximum denoising, full inheritance of staleness), and intermediate values balance the two. Our convergence analysis (Appendix E) shows that this blend interpolates between the two regimes monotonically.

Putting these pieces together, the spectral correction is an online, adaptive preconditioner whose basis and weights are estimated by the anchor circuit and updated as new anchor gradients arrive. The masked gradient is never discarded. Instead, it is softly pulled toward directions the anchor circuit has consistently observed. Because the anchor circuit runs asynchronously, this denoising signal arrives at the cost of staleness, not throughput.

3.3 Data-Parallel Compression

PP compression alone does not suffice in a decentralized mesh because dense DP synchronization can dominate wall-clock time and erase the gains from masking. At Internet-grade bandwidth the disparity is severe. We therefore compose PP compression with DP compression. In our implementation we use Streaming DiLoCo Douillard et al. (2025) with PowerSGD Vogels et al. (2019): PowerSGD reduces bytes per synchronization via low-rank gradient compression, DiLoCo reduces synchronization frequency by performing local steps between outer updates, and Streaming DiLoCo overlaps the outer synchronization with local computation. Note that our PP-side mechanism (activation masking and anchor priors) is independent of this particular DP compressor and can be combined with better alternatives.

3.4 End-to-End Training Procedure

The fast circuit performs most optimizer steps while the The anchor circuit periodically pulls recent layer shards from the fast circuit, runs unmasked forward–backward passes, and returns the resulting gradients asynchronously. When an anchor gradient arrives, the fast circuit updates the anchor momentum MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} and applies the spectral correction to subsequent masked gradients. The two-circuit design converts expensive unmasked computation into an asynchronous source of optimization geometry. The fast circuit retains the throughput benefits while the anchor circuit supplies delayed but reliable signals that stabilize the masked trajectory. Because the circuits are asynchronous, the system avoids the bandwidth spikes and pipeline stalls of synchronous unmasked steps. The overall system design is illustrated in Fig. 1

4 Convergence Analysis

We combine DP compression and PP activation masking. The DP component uses Streaming DiLoCo (Douillard et al., 2025) with PowerSGD (Vogels et al., 2019). We do not re-analyze this part: PowerSGD is a well-studied low-rank gradient compressor, while Streaming DiLoCo build on local-SGD/Federated-Averaging-style optimization. Both have been analyzed and validated extensively in prior work, and our method can in principle be paired with other DP compressors as well. We therefore focus on the masked activation training with asynchronous Anchor Priors.

Let F⁡(w)=𝔼ξ​[ℓ⁡(w,ξ)]F(w)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\ell(w;\xi)] denote the population training objective, F⋆F^{\star} its lower bound, wtw_{t} the model weights at step tt, η\eta the learning rate, and LL the smoothness constant of FF. Let GG bound the second moment of the update direction, and Δ\Delta the maximum staleness of anchor gradients in fast-circuit steps. The blend coefficient α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] controls how strongly the spectral correction is applied (Section 3).

Theorem 1 (Informal; full version in Appendix E).

Under standard smoothness and structural assumptions on the spectral filter, after TT steps,

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2≤2​(F⁡(w0)−F⋆)μα​η​T+Σα,Δ2+L​η​G2μα,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{2(F(w_{0})-F^{\star})}{\mu_{\alpha}\,\eta\,T}\;+\;\frac{\Sigma_{\alpha,\Delta}^{2}+L\eta G^{2}}{\mu_{\alpha}},

where Σα,Δ2\Sigma_{\alpha,\Delta}^{2} is a noise floor with three terms — unfiltered masked noise, filter-surviving noise (scaling as a contraction factor ρ<1\rho<1), and anchor staleness — and μα=1−(1−α)2​κ\mu_{\alpha}=1-(1-\alpha)^{2}\kappa measures how much true gradient the filter preserves (with κ∈[0,1)\kappa\in[0,1) the fraction of gradient energy the filter discards).

The bound has the standard nonconvex-SGD shape (a 1/T1/T term plus a noise floor) and improves over masked-only training when the filter contracts noise (ρ<1\rho<1) more than it suppresses signal (κ>0\kappa>0). Both quantities are small in the fine-tuning regime for two reasons: fine-tuning gradients live in a low-dimensional subspace (Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022), so the anchor basis preserves nearly all of ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) (κ\kappa small); and fine-tuning trajectories drift slowly (Neyshabur et al., 2020; Wortsman et al., 2022), so a delayed anchor basis remains close to the current one (staleness term controlled). Pretraining violates both, and the analysis correctly predicts no benefit there. The key takeaway is that the anchor gradients need not be exact synchronized updates, only good enough to estimate a low-rank subspace that is approximately preserved over the staleness window, the property the fine-tuning regime provides. The full proof is given in Appendix E.

5 Experiments

We evaluate the proposed system across diverse adaptation domains, including general knowledge, medical, programming, math, science, commonsense reasoning, summarization, and document parsing. We use PowerSGD (×64\times 64) and Streaming Diloco for DP. Our experiments span mesh sizes, model families, and model scales. We use A100 GPUs (40GB VRAM) for all our experiments.

5.1 Performance across different domain adaptation tasks

Table 1 summarizes the main domain-specific results. We use the publicly available Llama 3.2 1B checkpoint as the pretrained model: ∼\sim1.23B parameters, LLaMA-style decoder-only architecture with 1616 transformer layers, hidden dimension 20482048, and 3232 attention heads. All models are trained for 1010 epochs on the corresponding training datasets with learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, cosine decay, 22k context length, and batch size 3232. The system runs on a 7×87\times 8 mesh for the masked (fast) circuit and a 1×81\times 8 mesh for the unmasked (clean) circuit, with all inter-node links throttled to 200200 Mbps to emulate decentralized deployment. Datasets, evaluation metrics, and per-run configurations are in Appendix I.

As shown pure activation masking (M90, M95) is catastrophic on its own. Adding Anchor Priors reverses this collapse on every domain: M90+AP and M95+AP match the uncompressed Baseline within noise on most tasks and exceed it on several. We hypothesize the superior performance on some datasets might be due to the regularization effect of masking leading to better generalization. On the throughput, the system delivers substantially higher efficiency under bandwidth constraints: M95 reaches a ∼\sim45×\times TPS gain over the uncompressed baseline by stacking 20×20\times PP activation masking with 640×640\times DP gradient compression, while either compression alone yields only 1.4×1.4\times or 3.3×3.3\times because each merely shifts the bottleneck. We observe a practical delay of ∼20−25\sim 20-25 steps in the unmasked slow gradients.

5.2 Generalization across model variants

Table 3 reports results across Gemma, Qwen, Phi, LLaMA, and StableLM models, spanning 1B–8B parameters, 16–36 layers, and hidden dimensions from 1536 to 8192. We also evaluate the method across different DP×\timesPP mesh sizes. In all settings, we use 95% activation masking with Anchor Priors (AP). Across these variations, the proposed method consistently achieves near-parity with the uncompressed baseline, showcasing its generalization across architectures and scale.

5.3 Ablations

We sweep the two knobs that most directly govern the fast/clean trade-off: the activation-mask ratio pp and the Anchor-Prior staleness KK (number of fast-circuit steps between consecutive uncompressed priors). Table 2 reports results. Two failure modes emerge. First, p=99%p{=}99\% collapses at every KK. At this masking ratio the per-step information budget on the PP edges is too small for the clean prior to repair. Second, K=50K{=}50 collapses at every pp. By the time a prior this stale arrives, the masked trajectory has drifted beyond its effective correction horizon (Appendix H). Inside the operating envelope (p∈{90,95}%,K∈{10,20})(p\in\{90,95\}\%,\;K\in\{10,20\}) all four corners perform well. Finally, we ablate over τ\tau and α\alpha.

To verify that the method does not depend on a particular mesh topology, we sweep the DP ×\times PP grid from 4×44\times 4 up to 16×1616\times 16 under the same M95+AP and 200200 Mbps configuration as the main experiments. Table 6 reports MedQA, HumanEval, and GSM8K accuracy alongside aggregate throughput. As shown, the performance is stable across mesh sizes: all seven configurations land within ±5%\pm 5\% of the 8×88\times 8 reference on every metric, including the most-stressed 16×1616\times 16 case. The Anchor-Prior mechanism is therefore not tied to a specific topology. Second, throughput scales as expected: roughly linearly in DP−1\text{DP}{-}1 at fixed PP (more masked replicas trained in parallel), and inversely with TstepT_{\text{step}} along the PP axis (deeper pipelines move proportionally more masked activations per step). The combination of stable accuracy and predictable throughput scaling supports the claim that the fast/clean-circuit decomposition is a property of the algorithm rather than an artifact of a specific configuration.

5.4 Comparison to Activation-Communication Baselines

Table 5 compares M95+AP against published activation- and gradient-compression methods across medical (MedQA, MedMCQA), code (HumanEval, MBPP), and math (GSM8K) domains. Two findings stand out. First, prior methods do not survive at our compression target. Aggressive 2-bit quantization (AC-SGD, TAH-Quant) collapses entirely on generative tasks such as HumanEval, MBPP, and GSM8K, and reduces medical accuracy to near-random. Sparsification and 4-bit quantization recover partially. In contrast, our method matches or exceeds the uncompressed Baseline at 20×/20×20\times/20\times.

5.5 Robustness to Post-Hoc Pruning

A useful side-effect of training under aggressive activation masking is that the resulting checkpoint becomes more tolerant of post-hoc weight sparsification (Table 5). A plausible interpretation is that the masked-optimizer trajectory biases the trained weights toward solutions where information is distributed across many small-magnitude parameters, which is precisely what magnitude pruning rewards.

5.6 Reasoning and continual pretraining

Beyond per-domain fine-tuning, we test whether our method can sustain the longer training trajectories typical of continual pretraining and multi-stage SFT. We run a three-phase pipeline matching the SmolLM3 recipe on Llama-3.2-1B, : (1) reasoning-focused mid-training on Llama-Nemotron and OpenThoughts traces, (2) a first SFT round on the smoltalk2 mixture, and (3) a second SFT round on the same mixture. The masked optimization preserves reasoning capability, showing that the spectral correction tracks the true gradient across substantially longer trajectories than the per-domain fine-tuning runs. Total training is ∼60\sim 60B tokens. Full configurations in Appendix B. Learned reasoning traces are shown in Appendix C. Also, a natural concern with masked fine-tuning is whether it leaves the model in a state amenable to downstream RL. To this end, we perform an RL training on the checkpoints after the above steps and show that the compressed model does not affect the RL phase (Appendix D, Table 9).

6 Orthogonality to Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods reduce the number of trainable parameters and optimizer states, but they do not reduce pipeline-parallel activation traffic. Even when only LoRA adapters are trained, each pipeline stage still consumes the full forward and backward traffic. Thus, PEFT improves memory and update efficiency, whereas our method targets the orthogonal bottleneck of PP communication. To verify this, we evaluate dense SFT, LoRA, and our method, and their combination on the code domain. LoRA reduces trainable parameters but leaves performance relatively unchanged. The results are shown in Table 8.

7 Conclusion

We presented a communication-efficient system for decentralized LLM adaptation over low-bandwidth GPU meshes. By revisiting activation masking as an in-graph PP compression mechanism and pairing it with asynchronous Anchor Priors, adaptive spectral correction, and DP compression, our method makes sparse activation training practical even at extreme compression rates. The convergence analysis identifies the regime under which this works, i.e., low-dimensional, slowly-drifting gradient subspaces characteristic of fine-tuning, and explains why random PRF masking, rather than top-KK, is the right primitive in this setting. Across domain adaptation and continual pretraining, the resulting system matches or exceeds dense uncompressed training while delivering large throughput gains, and the resulting models are more robust to post-hoc pruning. These results show that post-pretraining adaptation can tolerate sparser intermediate signals than previously assumed, suggesting a practical path toward large-model adaptation over decentralized collections of low-end GPUs.

Limitations

Our experiments and analyis target the fine-tuning regime; we do not claim the method extends to pretraining, where gradient subspaces are high-dimensional and shift substantially over training. Adoptation of dual EMA optimizers such as Ademamix would be an interesting future direction (we have included a discussion in Appendix K). Further, our experiments are at the 11–88B parameter scale; scaling behavior at 7070B+ remains an open question.

Appendix B Reasoning and Continual-Pretraining Recipe

This section documents the three-phase training recipe used in Section 5.6. We follow the SmolLM3 methodology, but start from a smaller base model (Llama-3.2-1B) to make the experiment tractable at our compute budget.

B.1 Base model

We use Llama-3.2-1B as the starting point, with its tokenizer extended by SmolLM3 ChatML special tokens (<|im_start|>, <|im_end|>). The model is loaded in BF16 and trained with FlashAttention-2 throughout.

B.2 Phase 1: Reasoning mid-training

Data.

HuggingFaceTB/smoltalk2, config Mid:

    Llama_Nemotron_Post_Training_Dataset_reasoning_r1 (weight 1.01.0).

  • •

    OpenThoughts3_1.2M (weight 1.01.0).

Configuration.

Plain ChatML chat template (no system metadata, no thinking-mode header). AdamW with peak learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, cosine schedule with min-LR ratio 0.10.1, warmup ratio 0.030.03, gradient norm clipped at 0.20.2, sequence length 32,76832{,}768, packing enabled, 22 training epochs, gradient accumulation 22 on 8×8\times A100, Liger kernel enabled. No assistant-only loss masking in this phase; loss is computed over all tokens.

The smoltalk2 SFT mixture, comprising 25 splits with weights ranging from 0.020.02 to 1.01.0. Splits include conversational data (everyday conversations, system chats), instruction-following (Tulu-3 personas, OpenHermes-2.5), tool-use (Hermes function calling, xLAM, smolagents traces), reasoning traces (multi-turn-reasoning, Qwen3-32B-distilled think traces, s1k, OpenThoughts3 think variant), multilingual data (smoltalk multilingual, Aya), long-context (LongAlign 6464k), and structured data (table-GPT).

Data.

Identical to Phase 2 (same smoltalk2 SFT mixture and split weights).

Appendix C Reasoning Trace Examples

This appendix shows representative reasoning traces from the gshasiri/SmolLM3-Mid checkpoint after Phase 1 (reasoning mid-training) of the recipe in Section 5.6. Traces are produced with greedy decoding, enable_thinking=True, and max_new_tokens=600. Each example shows the full <think>...</think> block followed by the final answer.

Five examples below are the cleanly-correct answers from a 15-question simple-query batch. The remaining ten either produced incorrect answers or degenerated into repetition; this is expected because the SmolLM3-Mid checkpoint at this stage has chat-template scaffolding for thinking mode but has not yet undergone instruction/reasoning fine-tuning. The traces are intended to illustrate the format of the thinking output produced by the model after masked mid-training, not to demonstrate accuracy claims; per-task accuracy numbers are reported in Table 7.

C.1 Chat template

The SmolLM3 ChatML template used in Phases 2 and 3 injects per-turn system metadata (knowledge cutoff date, current date, reasoning mode /think or /no_think) and supports XML-style tool definitions. Reasoning content is wrapped in <think>...</think> tags. The template handles three reasoning regimes:

  • •

    System override: a system message containing /system_override replaces all metadata with user-supplied instructions verbatim.

  • •

    Think mode: assistant turns may include reasoning inside <think>...</think> tags. Used for splits ending in _think.

  • •

    No-think mode: assistant turns are emitted with an empty <think></think> block, signaling the model to skip reasoning. Used for splits ending in _no_think.

Phase 1 uses a simpler ChatML template without the metadata header, since the reasoning-trace data already encodes thinking-mode structure inline.

C.2 Activation masking and Anchor-Prior settings

Identical across all three phases and matching the per-domain experiments (Appendix I): activation mask probability 0.950.95, masking applied at layers {1,3,5,7,9,11,13}\{1,3,5,7,9,11,13\}. Anchor-Prior gradients are injected with the spectral filter described in Section 3. The results are reported in Table 7.

C.3 Evaluation

IFEval and GSM8K are evaluated via the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) on the final checkpoint after Phase 3. Token counts are measured as the cumulative training tokens across all three phases (sequence length ×\times optimizer steps ×\times effective batch).

Appendix D GSPO Reinforcement Learning Recipe

D.1 Reinforcement learning after masked SFT

A natural concern with masked fine-tuning is whether it leaves the model in a state amenable to downstream RL. Aggressive activation compression could in principle damage internal representations in ways that only manifest when the policy must be optimized against a sparse reward. For instance, by collapsing the entropy of intermediate features or by misaligning the model’s confidence estimates. We test this directly: starting from the M95+AP-trained final checkpoint of Section 5.6, we apply GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025) with a verifiable math reward on the Big-Math dataset and compare against the same RL run starting from the dense final checkpoint (Table 9).

The two starting points show essentially identical RL gains, and the post-RL gap matches the pre-RL gap. Masked SFT does not impair RL-amenability: the policy distribution remains entropic enough to explore, the reward landscape remains learnable, and the gradient signal from verifiable rewards translates into the same magnitude of capability gain whether the SFT trajectory was dense or communication-compressed.

Below we detail the GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025) configuration used in the RL phase. The setup follows VeRL’s reference GSPO recipe with adjustments for our 11B-parameter model and our context-length budget.

D.2 Pipeline

The full pipeline from base model to post-RL checkpoint is:

Llama-3.2-1B→Phase 1–3 SFTSFT model→DPODPO model→GSPOFinal policy\text{Llama-3.2-1B}\xrightarrow{\text{Phase 1--3 SFT}}\text{SFT model}\xrightarrow{\text{DPO}}\text{DPO model}\xrightarrow{\text{GSPO}}\text{Final policy}

We run this pipeline twice: once with dense SFT throughout, and once with M95+AP SFT throughout (Phases 1–3 of Appendix B). The DPO and GSPO phases are identical in both runs (same data, hyperparameters, and no masking), so any difference in the post-RL policy is attributable to the masked SFT trajectory.

D.3 Reward model

We use a verifiable math reward derived from the Big-Math dataset: each problem has a known final answer, and the reward is a binary indicator of whether the model’s extracted answer matches. We use the DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) reward manager, which adds a length-penalty buffer on top of the correctness signal: responses that exceed an overlong_buffer_len threshold within the maximum response length are linearly penalized down to a maximum penalty factor. This discourages reward hacking via verbose answers.

Settings.
  • •

    max_response_length: 7,6807{,}680 tokens (out of 8,1928{,}192-token total context, leaving 512512 for the prompt).

  • •

    overlong_buffer_len: 3,5843{,}584. Responses up to 7,680−3,584=4,0967{,}680-3{,}584=4{,}096 tokens incur no length penalty; beyond that, reward is linearly attenuated.

  • •

    overlong_penalty_factor: 1.01.0.

D.4 GSPO algorithm settings

Policy loss.

loss_mode = "gspo": GSPO’s sequence-level importance ratio, with loss aggregation seq-mean-token-mean (mean over tokens within a response, then mean over responses).

Advantage estimator.

adv_estimator = "grpo": group-relative advantage with no critic. Advantages are computed as the standardized rewards within each group of NN rollouts sharing a prompt.

Group size.

N=16N=16 responses per prompt.

Clip ratios.

Lower clip 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, upper clip 4×10−44\times 10^{-4}. These are substantially smaller than standard PPO clip ranges (0.20.2) because GSPO’s importance ratio is at the sequence level (the product of per-token ratios over a long response). A small per-sequence ratio window corresponds to a much larger effective per-token tolerance.

KL settings.

We disable both KL-in-reward and KL-as-loss (use_kl_in_reward = false, use_kl_loss = false). This is the standard RLVR setup where the only optimization signal is the verifiable reward.

D.5 Optimization

  • •

    Optimizer: AdamW, learning rate 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, weight decay 0.10.1, gradient clipping 1.01.0, warmup ratio 0.050.05. Entropy regularization disabled (entropy_coeff = 0).

  • •

    Train batch size: 3232 prompts per PPO iteration. With N=16N=16 rollouts each, this gives 512512 trajectories per update.

  • •

    PPO mini-batch: 1616 prompts (3232 mini-batches per outer iteration).

  • •

    Per-GPU micro-batch: 44 prompts.

  • •

    Dynamic batching enabled (use_dynamic_bsz = true), capping per-GPU tokens at 8,1928{,}192.

D.6 Rollout (vLLM)

  • •

    Backend: vLLM in asynchronous mode (rollouts overlap with actor training).

  • •

    GPU memory utilization for vLLM: 0.70.7.

  • •

    Tensor parallel: 11 (sufficient for a 11B model).

  • •

    Sampling for training rollouts: temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 1.01.0, top-kk disabled — maximally diverse exploration.

  • •

    Sampling for validation: temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.70.7, one sample per prompt — a slightly more conservative distribution for cleaner eval signal.

D.7 Training schedule

  • •

    22 epochs over Big-Math train split, with 2525-step validation cadence and 100100-step checkpoint cadence.

  • •

    No initial validation pass before training (val_before_train = false).

  • •

    DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 disabled in favor of FSDP; no parameter or optimizer offload (the 11B model fits comfortably on 4040 GB GPUs).

  • •

    Sequence parallelism disabled (sp_size = 1).

  • •

    Gradient checkpointing enabled.

D.8 Evaluation

GSM8K is evaluated via the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) on the final checkpoint after 22 epochs. We report exact-match accuracy at temperature 00 greedy decoding, matching the standard GSM8K evaluation protocol. Reported numbers are the best across all checkpoints of the corresponding run, with checkpoints saved every 100100 training steps.

Appendix E Convergence Analysis with Spectral Anchor Correction

We analyze a simplified version of our optimizer that captures the role of asynchronous anchor priors and spectral gradient correction. The analysis formalizes a single tradeoff: masked gradients are cheap but noisy, while unmasked anchor gradients are clean but delayed. The spectral filter built from the anchor momentum is the mechanism that trades one for the other. We work in the fine-tuning regime, where the optimization trajectory is short and the gradient subspace drifts slowly — the structural property that makes a delayed anchor basis useful.

E.1 Setup

Let F⁡(w)=𝔼ξ​[ℓ⁡(w,ξ)]F(w)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\ell(w;\xi)] denote the population objective. At iteration tt, the fast circuit computes a masked gradient gtmaskg_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}, and the anchor circuit asynchronously produces a delayed unmasked gradient gτancg_{\tau}^{\mathrm{anc}} from a stale snapshot wτw_{\tau} with t−τ≤Δt-\tau\leq\Delta. We use Δ\Delta for the maximum staleness in fast-circuit steps to avoid clashing with the DP replica count DD in Section 3.3.

For each matrix-valued parameter WW, we maintain an EMA anchor momentum

Mtanc=βanc​Mt−anc+(1−βanc)​gτanc,M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}=\beta_{\mathrm{anc}}\,M_{t^{-}}^{\mathrm{anc}}+(1-\beta_{\mathrm{anc}})\,g_{\tau}^{\mathrm{anc}},

updated each time a new anchor gradient arrives. Its SVD Mtanc=Ut​St​Vt⊤M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}=U_{t}S_{t}V_{t}^{\top} defines the spectral filter

di=sisi+λp,Dt=diag⁡(d1,…,dr),𝒫t​(G)=Ut​Dt​Ut⊤​G​Vt​Dt​Vt⊤,d_{i}=\frac{s_{i}}{s_{i}+\lambda_{p}},\qquad D_{t}=\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},\dots,d_{r}),\qquad\mathcal{P}_{t}(G)=U_{t}D_{t}U_{t}^{\top}\,G\,V_{t}D_{t}V_{t}^{\top},

where λp>0\lambda_{p}>0 is the spectral damping constant (distinct from the staleness index τ\tau). The update direction is ut=α​gtmask+(1−α)​𝒫t​(gtmask),u_{t}=\alpha\,g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathcal{P}_{t}(g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}), yielding wt+1=wt−η​utw_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta u_{t}.

E.2 Assumptions

Assumption 1 (Smoothness).

FF is LL-smooth and bounded below by F⋆F^{\star}.

Assumption 2 (Masked-gradient noise).

gtmask=∇F​(wt)+εtg_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}=\nabla F(w_{t})+\varepsilon_{t} where εt\varepsilon_{t} is generated by a fresh PRF mask draw at step tt, independent of all prior history. Conditional on that history, 𝔼​εt=0\mathbb{E}\,\varepsilon_{t}=0 and 𝔼​‖εt‖2≤σm2\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon_{t}\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{m}^{2}.

Assumption 3 (Delayed anchor gradients).

gτanc=∇F​(wτ)+ζτg_{\tau}^{\mathrm{anc}}=\nabla F(w_{\tau})+\zeta_{\tau} with t−τ≤Δt-\tau\leq\Delta, 𝔼​ζτ=0\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{\tau}=0, and 𝔼​‖ζτ‖2≤σa2\mathbb{E}\|\zeta_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{a}^{2}.

Assumption 4 (Bounded update).

𝔼​‖ut‖2≤G2\mathbb{E}\|u_{t}\|^{2}\leq G^{2} for all tt.

The next two assumptions describe what the spectral filter does to the signal and to the noise. They are the core structural conditions; we justify them in Section E.3 and quantify them in the supporting lemmas.

Assumption 5 (Signal preservation).

There exist κ∈[0,1)\kappa\in[0,1) and δΔstale≥0\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}\geq 0 such that

𝔼∥(I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)∥2≤κ𝔼∥∇F(wt)∥2+δΔstale.\mathbb{E}\bigl\|(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})\bigr\|^{2}\leq\kappa\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}+\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}.
Assumption 6 (Noise contraction).

There exists ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] such that 𝔼​‖𝒫t​εt‖2≤ρ​σm2.\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{P}_{t}\,\varepsilon_{t}\|^{2}\leq\rho\,\sigma_{m}^{2}.

E.3 Why these assumptions hold for fine-tuning

Both assumptions exploit two structural properties of fine-tuning that are well-documented in the literature: (i) fine-tuning gradients have low effective rank, and (ii) fine-tuning trajectories drift slowly in parameter space.

Low-rank gradient structure.

The intrinsic dimension of fine-tuning objectives is small (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021), the gradient and Hessian spectra during training are dominated by a handful of outlier directions (Gur-Ari et al., 2018; Papyan, 2020; Gressmann et al., 2020), and fine-tuning updates Δ​W=Wt−W0\Delta W=W_{t}-W_{0} are well approximated by low-rank matrices (Hu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2024; Lialin et al., 2023). Together these say ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) lies near a low-rank subspace, so the principal directions of MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} — itself an EMA of recent unmasked gradients — contain most of ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t})’s energy. This makes κ\kappa small (Assumption 5).

Slow weight drift.

Successful fine-tuning trajectories remain close to the pretrained initialization, with feature representations changing modestly (Neyshabur et al., 2020; Ramasesh et al., 2021), and fine-tuned checkpoints are close enough in parameter space to admit linear interpolation (Wortsman et al., 2022). Slow drift bounds the rotation of the gradient subspace between wτw_{\tau} and wtw_{t}, which controls δΔstale\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta} via a Davis–Kahan argument (Lemma 3).

Isotropic mask noise.

The mask mt,jm_{t,j} is drawn from a PRF whose seed is independent of model state, so εt\varepsilon_{t} is approximately isotropic in parameter space. A low-rank filter applied to isotropic noise contracts it strongly: ρ=O⁡(r2/(m​n))\rho=O(r^{2}/(mn)) in matrix dimensions m×nm\times n with effective rank rr (Lemma 2). This makes ρ\rho small (Assumption 6).

These properties fail in pretraining: the gradient subspace is high-dimensional and shifts substantially over a long trajectory. The analysis below predicts no benefit there, consistent with our empirical scoping of the method to fine-tuning workloads.

E.4 Supporting lemmas

Lemma 1 (Non-expansiveness of 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t}).

For any matrix GG, ‖𝒫t​(G)‖F≤‖G‖F\|\mathcal{P}_{t}(G)\|_{F}\leq\|G\|_{F}.

Proof.

Let PU=Ut​Dt​Ut⊤P_{U}=U_{t}D_{t}U_{t}^{\top} and PV=Vt​Dt​Vt⊤P_{V}=V_{t}D_{t}V_{t}^{\top}, so that 𝒫t​(G)=PU​G​PV\mathcal{P}_{t}(G)=P_{U}GP_{V}. Each filter weight satisfies 0≤di≤10\leq d_{i}\leq 1, so ‖Dt‖2≤1\|D_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1. Combined with the orthonormality of Ut,VtU_{t},V_{t}, this gives ‖PU‖2≤1\|P_{U}\|_{2}\leq 1 and ‖PV‖2≤1\|P_{V}\|_{2}\leq 1. Applying the submultiplicative inequality ‖A​G​B‖F≤‖A‖2​‖G‖F​‖B‖2\|AGB\|_{F}\leq\|A\|_{2}\|G\|_{F}\|B\|_{2} with A=PUA=P_{U}, B=PVB=P_{V}:

‖𝒫t​(G)‖F=‖PU​G​PV‖F≤‖PU‖2​‖G‖F​‖PV‖2≤‖G‖F.\|\mathcal{P}_{t}(G)\|_{F}=\|P_{U}GP_{V}\|_{F}\leq\|P_{U}\|_{2}\,\|G\|_{F}\,\|P_{V}\|_{2}\leq\|G\|_{F}.

∎

Lemma 2 (Noise contraction under matrix isotropy).

Suppose εt∈ℝm×n\varepsilon_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is matrix-isotropic with 𝔼⁡[vec⁡(εt)​vec​(εt)⊤]=(σm2/(m​n))​Im​n\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon_{t})\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon_{t})^{\top}]=(\sigma_{m}^{2}/(mn))\,I_{mn}, and that 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} is independent of εt\varepsilon_{t}. Then

𝔼​‖𝒫t​εt‖F2=σm2​reffU​reffVm​n,reffU=‖Dt‖F2=∑idi2,\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{P}_{t}\varepsilon_{t}\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{\sigma_{m}^{2}\,r_{\mathrm{eff}}^{U}\,r_{\mathrm{eff}}^{V}}{mn},\qquad r_{\mathrm{eff}}^{U}=\|D_{t}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2},

and similarly for reffVr_{\mathrm{eff}}^{V}. In particular, when the left and right filters share an effective rank rr in the sense reffU≈reffV≈rr_{\mathrm{eff}}^{U}\approx r_{\mathrm{eff}}^{V}\approx r with r≪min⁡(m,n)r\ll\min(m,n), we have ρ=O⁡(r2/(m​n))≪1\rho=O(r^{2}/(mn))\ll 1.

Proof.

Write 𝒫t​(εt)=PU​εt​PV\mathcal{P}_{t}(\varepsilon_{t})=P_{U}\varepsilon_{t}P_{V} as in Lemma 1. We compute the expected squared Frobenius norm in three steps.

Step 1: vectorize. Using the identity vec⁡(A​X​B)=(B⊤⊗A)​vec​(X)\mathrm{vec}(AXB)=(B^{\top}\otimes A)\,\mathrm{vec}(X),

vec⁡(PU​εt​PV)=(PV⊤⊗PU)​vec​(εt).\mathrm{vec}(P_{U}\varepsilon_{t}P_{V})=(P_{V}^{\top}\otimes P_{U})\,\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon_{t}).

Since ‖X‖F2=‖vec⁡(X)‖2\|X\|_{F}^{2}=\|\mathrm{vec}(X)\|^{2}, we have

‖PU​εt​PV‖F2=vec​(εt)⊤​(PV⊗PU⊤)​(PV⊤⊗PU)​vec​(εt).\|P_{U}\varepsilon_{t}P_{V}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon_{t})^{\top}(P_{V}\otimes P_{U}^{\top})(P_{V}^{\top}\otimes P_{U})\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon_{t}).

Step 2: take expectation. For any deterministic matrix MM and random vector xx with 𝔼⁡[x​x⊤]=c​I\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}]=cI, 𝔼⁡[x⊤​M​x]=c​tr​(M)\mathbb{E}[x^{\top}Mx]=c\,\mathrm{tr}(M). Applying this with c=σm2/(m​n)c=\sigma_{m}^{2}/(mn) and M=(PV⊗PU⊤)​(PV⊤⊗PU)M=(P_{V}\otimes P_{U}^{\top})(P_{V}^{\top}\otimes P_{U}),

𝔼​‖PU​εt​PV‖F2=σm2m​n​tr​((PV⊗PU⊤)​(PV⊤⊗PU)).\mathbb{E}\|P_{U}\varepsilon_{t}P_{V}\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{\sigma_{m}^{2}}{mn}\,\mathrm{tr}\!\bigl((P_{V}\otimes P_{U}^{\top})(P_{V}^{\top}\otimes P_{U})\bigr).

Step 3: simplify the trace. Using (A⊗B)​(C⊗D)=(A​C)⊗(B​D)(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AC)\otimes(BD) and tr⁡(A⊗B)=tr⁡(A)​tr​(B)\mathrm{tr}(A\otimes B)=\mathrm{tr}(A)\mathrm{tr}(B),

tr⁡((PV​PV⊤)⊗(PU⊤​PU))=tr⁡(PV​PV⊤)​tr​(PU⊤​PU)=‖PV‖F2​‖PU‖F2.\mathrm{tr}\!\bigl((P_{V}P_{V}^{\top})\otimes(P_{U}^{\top}P_{U})\bigr)=\mathrm{tr}(P_{V}P_{V}^{\top})\,\mathrm{tr}(P_{U}^{\top}P_{U})=\|P_{V}\|_{F}^{2}\,\|P_{U}\|_{F}^{2}.

Remark 1.

Strict matrix isotropy is idealized; the bound generalizes to anisotropic εt\varepsilon_{t} at the cost of a factor proportional to the largest covariance eigenvalue.

Lemma 3 (Subspace staleness via Davis–Kahan/Wedin).

Let M~t\widetilde{M}_{t} denote the anchor momentum that would result from an EMA of unmasked gradients evaluated at wtw_{t} (rather than at the stale {wτ}\{w_{\tau}\}), and let 𝒫~t\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t} be the filter built from M~t\widetilde{M}_{t}. Suppose MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} has singular value gap γ>0\gamma>0 between its rrth and (r+1)(r{+}1)th singular values, and 𝔼​‖Mtanc−M~t‖F2≤Et\mathbb{E}\|M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}-\widetilde{M}_{t}\|_{F}^{2}\leq E_{t}. Then there is a constant cdk>0c_{\mathrm{dk}}>0 such that

𝔼∥(𝒫t−𝒫~t)∇F(wt)∥2≤cdk​Etγ2⋅𝔼∥∇F(wt)∥2.\mathbb{E}\bigl\|(\mathcal{P}_{t}-\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})\bigr\|^{2}\leq\frac{c_{\mathrm{dk}}\,E_{t}}{\gamma^{2}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}.

Under LL-smoothness, bounded delay Δ\Delta, and bounded update norm GG,

Et≤2​L2​η2​Δ2​G2+2​σa2.E_{t}\leq 2L^{2}\eta^{2}\Delta^{2}G^{2}+2\sigma_{a}^{2}.
Sketch.

By Wedin’s sin⁡Θ\sin\Theta theorem (Wedin, 1972; Yu et al., 2015), the principal left- and right-singular subspaces of MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} and M~t\widetilde{M}_{t} differ in Frobenius norm by at most c​‖Mtanc−M~t‖F/γc\,\|M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}}-\widetilde{M}_{t}\|_{F}/\gamma. The spectral filter 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} is Lipschitz in those subspaces and in the singular values sis_{i} (the map s↦s/(s+λp)s\mapsto s/(s+\lambda_{p}) is 1/λp1/\lambda_{p}-Lipschitz), so applying these Lipschitz bounds to the filter difference gives the first claim with cdkc_{\mathrm{dk}} absorbing the Wedin and Lipschitz constants.

For the bound on EtE_{t}: the discrepancy M~t−Mtanc\widetilde{M}_{t}-M_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} is a weighted average of differences ∇F​(wt)−gτanc=(∇F​(wt)−∇F​(wτ))−ζτ\nabla F(w_{t})-g_{\tau}^{\mathrm{anc}}=(\nabla F(w_{t})-\nabla F(w_{\tau}))-\zeta_{\tau}. The first term is bounded by L​‖wt−wτ‖≤L​η​Δ​GL\|w_{t}-w_{\tau}\|\leq L\eta\Delta G (LL-smoothness and bounded update norm); the second has expected squared norm at most σa2\sigma_{a}^{2}. Squaring and applying ‖a−b‖2≤2​‖a‖2+2​‖b‖2\|a-b\|^{2}\leq 2\|a\|^{2}+2\|b\|^{2} yields the stated bound on EtE_{t}. ∎

Corollary 1 (Bound on δΔstale\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}).

Suppose 𝒫~t\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t} acts as identity on ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) up to residual κ0​𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2\kappa_{0}\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2} (the low-intrinsic-rank hypothesis). Then Assumption 5 holds with

κ=2​κ0+4​cdk​L2​η2​Δ2​G2γ2,δΔstale=4​cdk​σa2γ2​supt𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2.\kappa=2\kappa_{0}+\frac{4c_{\mathrm{dk}}L^{2}\eta^{2}\Delta^{2}G^{2}}{\gamma^{2}},\qquad\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}=\frac{4c_{\mathrm{dk}}\,\sigma_{a}^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\sup_{t}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}.
Proof.

We split (I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t}) into a fresh-anchor part and a staleness part by inserting and subtracting 𝒫~t\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t}:

(I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)=(I−𝒫~t)∇F(wt)+(𝒫~t−𝒫t)∇F(wt).(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})=(I-\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})+(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t}-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t}).

Applying ‖a+b‖2≤2​‖a‖2+2​‖b‖2\|a+b\|^{2}\leq 2\|a\|^{2}+2\|b\|^{2} and taking expectations,

𝔼∥(I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)∥2≤2𝔼∥(I−𝒫~t)∇F(wt)∥2+2𝔼∥(𝒫~t−𝒫t)∇F(wt)∥2.\mathbb{E}\|(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}\leq 2\mathbb{E}\|(I-\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\|(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{t}-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}.

The first term is bounded by 2​κ0​𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖22\kappa_{0}\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2} by hypothesis. The second is bounded by Lemma 3, with Et≤2​L2​η2​Δ2​G2+2​σa2E_{t}\leq 2L^{2}\eta^{2}\Delta^{2}G^{2}+2\sigma_{a}^{2}. Combining gives the claim. ∎

The corollary makes the dependence transparent: κ0\kappa_{0} measures how well the gradient lies in the anchor’s principal subspace at the current weights (small in fine-tuning, large in pretraining), while the remaining terms measure subspace rotation due to delay and anchor noise, both governed by the gap γ\gamma.

E.5 Main result

Theorem 2 (Convergence with spectral anchor priors).

Suppose Assumptions 1–6 hold. Define

μα=1−(1−α)2​κ,Σα,Δ2=2​α2​σm2+2​(1−α)2​ρ​σm2+(1−α)2​δΔstale.\mu_{\alpha}=1-(1-\alpha)^{2}\kappa,\qquad\Sigma_{\alpha,\Delta}^{2}=2\alpha^{2}\sigma_{m}^{2}+2(1-\alpha)^{2}\rho\,\sigma_{m}^{2}+(1-\alpha)^{2}\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}.

Assume κ<1/(1−α)2\kappa<1/(1-\alpha)^{2} so μα>0\mu_{\alpha}>0, and choose η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L. Then after TT iterations,

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2≤2​(F⁡(w0)−F⋆)μα​η​T+Σα,Δ2+L​η​G2μα.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2(F(w_{0})-F^{\star})}{\mu_{\alpha}\,\eta\,T}+\frac{\Sigma_{\alpha,\Delta}^{2}+L\eta G^{2}}{\mu_{\alpha}}.
Reading the bound.

Three contributions to the noise floor: α2​σm2\alpha^{2}\sigma_{m}^{2} (unfiltered masked noise), (1−α)2​ρ​σm2(1-\alpha)^{2}\rho\sigma_{m}^{2} (the masked noise that survives spectral filtering, small by Lemma 2), and (1−α)2​δΔstale(1-\alpha)^{2}\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta} (anchor noise plus subspace staleness, small by Lemma 3 when γ\gamma is nontrivial). The factor 1/μα1/\mu_{\alpha} on the rate makes explicit the cost of the filter discarding part of the true gradient. In fine-tuning, κ\kappa and ρ\rho are small and γ\gamma is bounded away from zero, so the bound improves over masked-only training (recovered at α=1\alpha=1, where μα=1\mu_{\alpha}=1).

E.6 Proof of Theorem 2

The proof has four parts: a one-step descent inequality from LL-smoothness, a decomposition of the update direction utu_{t} into a true-gradient term plus a deterministic bias and a zero-mean noise, a bound on the bias term that produces the μα\mu_{\alpha} factor, and a telescoping sum.

Part 1: one-step descent from LL-smoothness.

LL-smoothness of FF gives the standard inequality

F⁡(wt+1)≤F⁡(wt)+⟨∇F​(wt),wt+1−wt⟩+L2​‖wt+1−wt‖2.F(w_{t+1})\leq F(w_{t})+\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),w_{t+1}-w_{t}\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}.

Substituting the update wt+1−wt=−η​utw_{t+1}-w_{t}=-\eta u_{t} and taking expectations, then using 𝔼​‖ut‖2≤G2\mathbb{E}\|u_{t}\|^{2}\leq G^{2} (Assumption 4) on the quadratic term:

𝔼​F​(wt+1)≤𝔼​F​(wt)−η​𝔼​⟨∇F​(wt),ut⟩+L​η22​G2.\mathbb{E}F(w_{t+1})\leq\mathbb{E}F(w_{t})-\eta\,\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),u_{t}\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}G^{2}. (4)

The remaining work is to lower-bound the inner-product term 𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),ut⟩\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),u_{t}\rangle in terms of 𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}, so that we can extract a usable descent quantity.

Part 2: decomposing utu_{t} into signal, bias, and noise.

Recall ut=α​gtmask+(1−α)​𝒫t​(gtmask)u_{t}=\alpha g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{P}_{t}(g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}). Substituting gtmask=∇F​(wt)+εtg_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}=\nabla F(w_{t})+\varepsilon_{t} (Assumption 2) and grouping deterministic (∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t})-dependent) terms separately from stochastic (εt\varepsilon_{t}-dependent) terms,

ut=α∇F(wt)+(1−α)𝒫t∇F(wt)⏟deterministic+α​εt+(1−α)​𝒫t​εt⏟nt.u_{t}=\underbrace{\alpha\,\nabla F(w_{t})+(1-\alpha)\,\mathcal{P}_{t}\,\nabla F(w_{t})}_{\text{deterministic}}\;+\;\underbrace{\alpha\,\varepsilon_{t}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathcal{P}_{t}\,\varepsilon_{t}}_{n_{t}}.

Adding and subtracting (1−α)∇F(wt)(1-\alpha)\nabla F(w_{t}) in the deterministic part to extract ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) explicitly,

ut=∇F​(wt)−(1−α)(I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)⏟bt+nt.u_{t}=\nabla F(w_{t})-\underbrace{(1-\alpha)(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t})}_{b_{t}}+n_{t}.

Substituting this into the inner product,

𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),ut⟩=𝔼​‖∇F​(wt)‖2−𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),bt⟩+𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩.\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),u_{t}\rangle=\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}-\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),b_{t}\rangle+\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle. (5)

We now show the third term on the right vanishes.

The cross term 𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle is zero.

This step needs care: 𝔼⁡[nt]=0\mathbb{E}[n_{t}]=0 alone does not imply 𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩=0\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle=0, because ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) is itself random and could be correlated with ntn_{t}. The argument uses conditioning. Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} denote the history through the start of step tt: the iterates w0,…,wtw_{0},\dots,w_{t}, all past mask noise, and all anchor gradients received before step tt. By the tower property of expectation,

𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩∣ℱt]].\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\,\bigr].

Conditional on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, two things hold:

  1. 1.

    ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) is a deterministic function of wtw_{t}, which is in ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. So ∇F​(wt)\nabla F(w_{t}) is a constant inside the inner conditional expectation, and we can pull it out:

    𝔼⁡[⟨∇F​(wt),nt⟩∣ℱt]=⟨∇F​(wt),𝔼⁡[nt∣ℱt]⟩.\mathbb{E}[\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),n_{t}\rangle\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),\,\mathbb{E}[n_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\rangle.
  2. 2.

    𝔼⁡[nt∣ℱt]=0\mathbb{E}[n_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0. To see this: ntn_{t} is a linear function of εt\varepsilon_{t}, with coefficient operators that are functions of 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t}. E.7 Discussion

The convergence neighborhood splits into three interpretable terms: unfiltered masked noise α2​σm2\alpha^{2}\sigma_{m}^{2}, filter-surviving noise (1−α)2​ρ​σm2(1-\alpha)^{2}\rho\sigma_{m}^{2}, and anchor-staleness (1−α)2​δΔstale(1-\alpha)^{2}\delta^{\mathrm{stale}}_{\Delta}. The rate factor 1/μα1/\mu_{\alpha} encodes the cost of signal suppression. The result recovers masked-only training at α=1\alpha=1 (μα=1\mu_{\alpha}=1, no filter) and improves on it whenever the filter contracts noise (ρ<1\rho<1) more than it suppresses signal (κ>0\kappa>0), i.e., precisely the fine-tuning regime described in Section E.3.

In pretraining or with aggressive learning rates, Δ\Delta grows, the gap γ\gamma shrinks, and κ\kappa approaches its upper limit; the filter both keeps less signal and inherits more staleness. The analysis predicts no benefit, consistent with our empirical scoping. At the opposite extreme of high-bandwidth links the masking is unnecessary in the first place; this analysis is specifically relevant when the fast circuit is communication-bound and the anchor circuit can run asynchronously — the Δ≈20\Delta\approx 20–2525 regime characterized in the staleness analysis of Section H.

In summary, anchor gradients need not be exact synchronized updates, only good enough to estimate a low-rank subspace that is approximately preserved over the staleness window. Fine-tuning is precisely the regime where this is true.

Appendix F Why Random Masking and Not Top-KK?

A natural alternative to PRF-based random masking is top-KK selection, where each token retains the KK activation entries of largest magnitude (or, on the backward pass, the KK largest entries of the activation gradient). Top-KK is the dominant sparsification scheme in data-parallel gradient compression (Lin et al., 2018; Aji and Heafield, 2017; Alistarh et al., 2018), where it is typically combined with error feedback to recover unbiasedness (Karimireddy et al., 2019; Stich et al., 2018). We deliberately do not use top-KK for PP activation compression. This subsection explains why, and shows that the choice is not systematic: random masking is required for the convergence analysis of Section E to apply, and it is also the scheme under which the spectral anchor filter is most effective (even empirically). Below, we provide a systematic analysis on this.

Setup.

Let h∈ℝT×Hh\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H} denote a hidden-state tensor at a masked PP boundary, and let h~=h⊙m\tilde{h}=h\odot m denote the transmitted activation under mask m∈{0,1}T×Hm\in\{0,1\}^{T\times H} with retention fraction 1−p1-p. Two schemes:

  • •

    Random masking (ours). mt,j∼Bernoulli⁡(1−p)m_{t,j}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-p), independent across (t,j)(t,j), generated by a shared PRF independent of the model state. With the standard rescaling h~←h~/(1−p)\tilde{h}\leftarrow\tilde{h}/(1-p) absorbed at the receiver, 𝔼m​[h~]=h\mathbb{E}_{m}[\tilde{h}]=h.

  • •

    Top-KK masking. mt,j=𝟙[|ht,j|∈top-K(ht,:)]m_{t,j}=\mathbb{1}[|h_{t,j}|\in\mathrm{top}\text{-}K(h_{t,:})]. The mask is a deterministic function of hh.

Unbiasedness and the convergence theorem

The masked-gradient noise εt=gtmask−∇F​(wt)\varepsilon_{t}=g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}-\nabla F(w_{t}) enters the descent inequality through the decomposition ut=∇F​(wt)−bt+ntu_{t}=\nabla F(w_{t})-b_{t}+n_{t}, with the requirement 𝔼⁡[nt∣ℱt]=0\mathbb{E}[n_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0 (Section E, proof of Theorem 2). This in turn relies on 𝔼⁡[εt∣ℱt]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0 (Assumption 2). We now show that random masking satisfies this property while top-KK does not.

Proposition 1 (Unbiasedness of random masking).

Under random masking with the standard rescaling, the masked activation satisfies 𝔼m​[h~]=h\mathbb{E}_{m}[\tilde{h}]=h. Consequently, for any downstream function of h~\tilde{h} that is linear in h~\tilde{h} at first order (in particular, the gradient computation through the masked PP boundary in expectation), the resulting masked gradient satisfies 𝔼⁡[gtmask∣ℱt]=∇F​(wt).\mathbb{E}[g_{t}^{\mathrm{mask}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\nabla F(w_{t}). The mask mm is generated by a PRF whose seed is independent of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, so εt\varepsilon_{t} has zero conditional mean.

Sketch.

Each coordinate satisfies 𝔼m​[h~t,j]=(1−p)⋅ht,j/(1−p)=ht,j\mathbb{E}_{m}[\tilde{h}_{t,j}]=(1-p)\cdot h_{t,j}/(1-p)=h_{t,j}, by the rescaling. The PRF is a function of (ℓ,t,B,S,H)(\ell,t,B,S,H) but not of hh or wtw_{t}, so the mask is independent of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. Hence the noise inherited by any function evaluated at h~\tilde{h} has zero conditional mean to leading order in the rescaled deviation h~−h\tilde{h}-h. ∎

Proposition 2 (Bias of top-KK masking).

Under top-KK masking, the masked activation satisfies 𝔼⁡[h~∣ℱt]=h⊙mtop​-​K​(h)≠h\mathbb{E}[\tilde{h}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=h\odot m_{\mathrm{top}\text{-}K}(h)\neq h in general, since the mask is a deterministic function of hh (and hh is itself ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable). The residual h−h~h-\tilde{h} is the bottom-(H−K)(H{-}K) magnitude entries of hh, which is a deterministic, non-zero function of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. Therefore 𝔼⁡[εt∣ℱt]≠0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\neq 0, and Assumption 2 fails.

Remark 2 (Failure mode in the descent inequality).

Suppose top-KK masking is used. Decomposing the masked gradient as gttopK=∇F​(wt)−bttopK+nt′,g_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}=\nabla F(w_{t})-b_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}+n_{t}^{\prime}, where bttopK=𝔼⁡[∇F​(wt)−gttopK∣ℱt]b_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}=\mathbb{E}[\nabla F(w_{t})-g_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}] is the state-dependent bias and nt′n_{t}^{\prime} is the residual stochastic component, the inner-product term in the smoothness expansion becomes

𝔼⁡⟨∇F​(wt),ut⟩=‖∇F​(wt)‖2−⟨∇F​(wt),btfilter+α​bttopK⟩,\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),u_{t}\rangle=\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|^{2}-\langle\nabla F(w_{t}),b_{t}^{\mathrm{filter}}+\alpha b_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}\rangle,

where btfilter=(1−α)(I−𝒫t)∇F(wt)b_{t}^{\mathrm{filter}}=(1-\alpha)(I-\mathcal{P}_{t})\nabla F(w_{t}). Unlike btfilterb_{t}^{\mathrm{filter}}, the bias bttopKb_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}} is not controlled by Assumption 5: it does not lie in the principal subspace of MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} in any structured way, because top-KK selects on activation magnitude, not on the gradient geometry the anchor circuit observes through unmasked passes. The spectral filter 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} therefore cannot remove it, and the bias propagates through the telescoping sum in the proof as an additive non-vanishing term of order η​T⋅𝔼​‖bttopK‖2\eta T\cdot\mathbb{E}\|b_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}}\|^{2}. The convergence neighborhood acquires a floor that does not shrink with TT and that the anchor circuit cannot reduce.

Why error feedback does not save top-KK at PP boundaries.

In data-parallel gradient compression, the bias of top-KK is corrected by error feedback (Karimireddy et al., 2019; Stich et al., 2018): the unsent residual is accumulated in a memory buffer and added to the next step’s gradient before compression. Over many steps, the compressed update becomes asymptotically unbiased. This works in the DP setting because the residual is associated with a parameter and is meaningful across optimizer steps.

At a PP activation boundary, the residual is associated with an activation on a particular microbatch. Two obstructions prevent its reuse:

(i) Activations are step-local. The residual ht−h~th_{t}-\tilde{h}_{t} is computed from the inputs xtx_{t} and the current weights wtw_{t}. At step t+1t{+}1 the inputs are xt+1≠xtx_{t+1}\neq x_{t} and the weights are wt+1≠wtw_{t+1}\neq w_{t}, so ht+1h_{t+1} is an entirely different tensor and the residual from step tt has no natural reinjection point.

(ii) Forward/backward sparsity patterns coincide. Section 3.1 shows that in-graph masking forces the backward gradient to inherit the same sparsity pattern as the forward activation. With top-KK, the forward retains coordinates of largest |ht,j||h_{t,j}|, but the gradient ∂ℒ/∂ht,j\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h_{t,j} is not in general largest at the same coordinates. Either the backward pattern is forced to match the forward (losing the largest gradient entries, defeating the purpose of top-KK), or the patterns are decoupled (losing the in-graph property and requiring separate metadata transmission). Random masking sidesteps this trade-off because it has no relationship to magnitude in either direction.

These obstructions are specific to PP activation compression, not a general statement about top-KK. Top-KK remains an effective DP compressor, and indeed our system uses PowerSGD-style compression along the DP axis (Section 3.3). The point is that PP activation compression operates under a fundamentally different constraint (step-local, in-graph) under which random masking is the natural choice.

Compatibility with the spectral filter

Beyond unbiasedness, the spectral anchor filter denoises masked gradients only when the noise is approximately isotropic relative to the anchor basis (Lemma 2). The two schemes differ sharply on this criterion.

Proposition 3 (Approximate isotropy of random-mask noise).

Under random masking with retention probability 1−p1-p and standard rescaling, the per-coordinate noise satisfies

𝔼⁡[εt,j∣ℱt]=0,Var⁡(εt,j∣ℱt)=p1−p​ht,j2,\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_{t,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t})=\frac{p}{1-p}\,h_{t,j}^{2},

where the conditioning on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} subsumes conditioning on the current activation hh (which is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable through wtw_{t} and the inputs), and the entries are independent across jj. If activations across the hidden dimension have approximately uniform second moment, εt\varepsilon_{t} is approximately matrix-isotropic in the sense of Lemma 2, and the spectral filter contracts noise by a factor ρ=O⁡(r2/(m​n))\rho=O(r^{2}/(mn)) where rr is the effective rank of the filter.

Proposition 4 (Anti-isotropy of top-KK noise).

Under top-KK masking, the residual h−h~h-\tilde{h} has support exactly on the bottom-(H−K)(H{-}K) coordinates of hh in magnitude. Therefore the noise is concentrated in low-magnitude directions, anti-correlated with the signal, and not isotropic. The covariance Cov⁡(εt)\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_{t}) has rank H−KH-K and is supported on a subspace orthogonal to the dominant activation directions.

Implication for the filter.

The anchor momentum MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} is built from unmasked gradients, which reflect the dominant gradient geometry of the task. In fine-tuning, this geometry is low-rank and aligned with the high-magnitude directions of activations and of ∂ℒ/∂h\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h (by the intrinsic-dimensionality literature cited in Section E.3). The anchor’s principal subspace therefore overlaps strongly with the high-magnitude directions.

Under random masking, the noise εt\varepsilon_{t} is isotropic and the filter contracts it: low-rank 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} acting on isotropic noise gives ρ=O⁡(r2/(m​n))\rho=O(r^{2}/(mn)) as in Lemma 2. Under top-KK, the noise lives precisely in the complementary subspace — the low-magnitude directions the anchor basis does not span. The filter 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} would correctly suppress this noise (it has no projection onto the anchor’s principal subspace), but it would also suppress nothing useful in exchange: the noise was already orthogonal to the signal directions the filter preserves. The “denoising” effect would be illusory, i.e., the filter cannot remove noise it never sees, and the masked-step bias bttopKb_{t}^{\mathrm{topK}} propagates through unaffected.

Summary

The choice of random masking over top-KK is forced by two compounding requirements:

  1. 1.

    Unbiasedness without error feedback. Random masking is conditionally unbiased on activation gradients; top-KK is biased and the natural correction (error feedback) is unavailable at PP activation boundaries because the residual is step-local and in-graph forward/backward sparsity must coincide.

  2. 2.

    Isotropy relative to the anchor basis. The spectral anchor filter denoises isotropic noise efficiently (Lemma 2) but cannot interact usefully with the structured low-magnitude noise produced by top-KK.

Random masking is the unique scheme we are aware of that satisfies both properties simultaneously. The convergence analysis of Section E relies on the first; the empirical effectiveness of the spectral filter relies on the second. Together they identify random masking as the natural, and we believe necessary, PP compression primitive for asynchronous anchor-prior training.

Figure 2 reports the alignment ηr=‖U⊤​g​V‖F2/‖g‖F2\eta_{r}=\|U^{\top}g\,V\|_{F}^{2}/\|g\|_{F}^{2} of the unmasked gradient with the rank-rr principal subspace of the anchor momentum, at 6161 snapshots spanning 15001500 training steps, for r∈{16,64,256}r\in\{16,64,256\}. The FT trajectory, starting from the uncompressed code-domain checkpoint and continuing under unclipped Adam, keeps η64FT\eta_{64}^{\rm FT} stable around 0.170.17–0.190.19 throughout the horizon. The PT trajectory, starting from random init under the same data and optimizer, drops from η64PT≈0.13\eta_{64}^{\rm PT}\approx 0.13 early in training to ∼0.08\sim 0.08 in the latter half and continues to decay.
