The constant κ\kappa that bounds out-of-subspace bias is materially smaller in fine-tuning than in pretraining-from-random-init, and that gap is sustained across the entire training horizon the AP correction has to operate over — empirically validating the assumption justifications in Section E.3 and the no-benefit-in-pretraining caveat that follows from them.

Appendix H Staleness of the Anchor Prior

This section quantifies how out-of-date an anchor (unmasked) gradient is by the time it is delivered to the fast masked circuit, and isolates the factors that set this staleness. The analysis is instantiated for the configuration used in our throughput study (Section 3.3): a 1.21.2B-parameter model in BF16 over 88 pipeline-parallel stages and 88 data-parallel replicas, connected by 200200 Mbps point-to-point links (≈25\approx 25 MB/s of useful payload). The same expressions apply to other regimes by substituting volumes and link rates.

H.1 Anchor circuit cycle time

Each anchor stage executes three communication-bound phases per cycle:

  1. 1.

    Weight pull. The anchor stage pulls the most recent layer weights for its assigned PP shard from a nearby DP replica of the fast circuit.

  2. 2.

    Unmasked forward–backward. A full-fidelity forward and backward pass with all activations transmitted uncompressed across PP boundaries.

  3. 3.

    Gradient push. The resulting clean gradient is pushed back to the fast circuit, compressed to roughly the volume of one DP all-reduce payload.

Let TpullT_{\mathrm{pull}}, TcleanT_{\mathrm{clean}}, TpushT_{\mathrm{push}} denote the wall-clock times of these three phases, and TmaskT_{\mathrm{mask}} denote one masked step on the fast circuit. The anchor gradient delivered at the end of the cycle was computed from weights pulled at the start of phase 2, so its staleness measured in fast-circuit steps is

Kstale=Tpull+Tclean+TpushTmask.K_{\mathrm{stale}}\;=\;\frac{T_{\mathrm{pull}}+T_{\mathrm{clean}}+T_{\mathrm{push}}}{T_{\mathrm{mask}}}. (9)

The numerator is the anchor cycle time; the denominator is the fast-circuit cycle time.

H.2 Numbers for the 200 Mbps configuration

We instantiate Eq. (9) for sequence length S=2048S{=}2048, hidden size H=2048H{=}2048, and 1616 microbatches per optimizer step, with DP communication compressed via PowerSGD (64×64\times) and amortized via DiLoCo with local horizon K=10K{=}10.

Weight pull.

Each anchor stage holds 1.2​B/8=1501.2\mathrm{B}/8=150M parameters. In BF16 this is 300300 MB per stage: Tpull≈300​MB/25​MB/s=12​s.T_{\mathrm{pull}}\approx 300\penalty\ \mathrm{MB}/25\penalty\ \mathrm{MB/s}=12\penalty\ \mathrm{s}.

Unmasked forward–backward.

At each PP boundary, the activation tensor per microbatch is S⋅H⋅2=8S\!\cdot\!H\!\cdot\!2=8 MB. With 77 boundaries, 1616 microbatches, and forward and backward traversals, the total unmasked PP volume per step is 2⋅7⋅16⋅8​MB≈1.82\cdot 7\cdot 16\cdot 8\penalty\ \mathrm{MB}\approx 1.8 GB: Tclean≈1.8​GB/25​MB/s≈72​s.T_{\mathrm{clean}}\approx 1.8\penalty\ \mathrm{GB}/25\penalty\ \mathrm{MB/s}\approx 72\penalty\ \mathrm{s}.

Gradient push.

The compressed anchor gradient is on the order of one PowerSGD-compressed all-reduce payload, ∼30\sim 30–4040 MB per stage, giving Tpush≈1T_{\mathrm{push}}\approx 1–22 s.

Masked-step time.

The masked step incurs 1−p=5%1{-}p=5\% of the unmasked PP volume, plus the compressed and amortized DP all-reduce, plus a small compute term that is dominated by communication in this regime:

Tmask≈Tclean20+N⋅bgrad/64B⋅K+ϵ≈ 3.6+0.15+ϵ≈ 3.8​s.T_{\mathrm{mask}}\;\approx\;\frac{T_{\mathrm{clean}}}{20}\;+\;\frac{N\cdot b_{\mathrm{grad}}/64}{B\cdot K}\;+\;\epsilon\;\approx\;3.6+0.15+\epsilon\;\approx\;3.8\penalty\ \mathrm{s}.
Resulting staleness.

Kstale≈(12+72+2)/3.8≈23K_{\mathrm{stale}}\approx(12+72+2)/3.8\approx 23 masked steps. Of these, ∼20\sim 20 steps come from the unmasked PP pass itself (Tclean/TmaskT_{\mathrm{clean}}/T_{\mathrm{mask}}, which equals the masking ratio 1/(1−p)=201/(1-p)=20), and ∼3\sim 3 come from the weight pull. This matches with the 20−2520-25 step delay we practically observed.

H.3 Decomposition

Eq. (9) separates into two terms with distinct scaling:

Kstale=TcleanTmask⏟PP-ratio+Tpull+TpushTmask⏟weight-refresh.K_{\mathrm{stale}}\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{T_{\mathrm{clean}}}{T_{\mathrm{mask}}}}_{\text{PP-ratio}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{T_{\mathrm{pull}}+T_{\mathrm{push}}}{T_{\mathrm{mask}}}}_{\text{weight-refresh}}. (10)

The PP-ratio term equals the activation-mask ratio 1/(1−p)1/(1-p) in the PP-bound regime: 2020 at 95%95\% masking, 1010 at 90%90\%, 100100 at 99%99\%. It is unaffected by DP compression because both circuits run the same forward–backward computation and differ only in PP payload size. The weight-refresh term is set by the cost of synchronizing the anchor’s weights with the fast circuit; at 300300 MB per stage and 2525 MB/s, it contributes ∼3\sim 3 steps. The PP-ratio term dominates in this regime.

H.4 Hiding the weight-refresh term via overlap

The weight-refresh term is hideable. If the anchor circuit pipelines the weight pull for cycle i+1i{+}1 behind the unmasked forward–backward of cycle ii,

Tcycleoverlap=max⁡(Tpull,Tclean+Tpush)≈TcleanT_{\mathrm{cycle}}^{\mathrm{overlap}}\;=\;\max\bigl(T_{\mathrm{pull}},\;T_{\mathrm{clean}}+T_{\mathrm{push}}\bigr)\;\approx\;T_{\mathrm{clean}}

since Tpull≪TcleanT_{\mathrm{pull}}\ll T_{\mathrm{clean}}. Staleness then reduces to the PP-ratio term alone:

Kstaleoverlap≈TcleanTmask≈ 20​masked steps,K_{\mathrm{stale}}^{\mathrm{overlap}}\;\approx\;\frac{T_{\mathrm{clean}}}{T_{\mathrm{mask}}}\;\approx\;20\penalty\ \text{masked steps},

matching the cadence of a synchronous formulation that takes one full unmasked update every 2020 masked steps. The asynchronous variant hides this latency inside the fast pipeline rather than blocking on it.

H.5 Sensitivity to other regimes

Equation (10) makes the regime dependence of staleness explicit:

Mask rate.

Increasing the mask rate pp shrinks TmaskT_{\mathrm{mask}} but leaves TcleanT_{\mathrm{clean}} unchanged. The PP-ratio term grows as 1/(1−p)1/(1-p): Kstale≈100K_{\mathrm{stale}}\approx 100 at p=99%p=99\%, and ≈200\approx 200 at p=99.5%p=99.5\%. The anchor prior remains useful only when the optimization landscape changes slowly relative to this horizon.

Link bandwidth.

The PP-ratio term is invariant under uniform bandwidth scaling, since all communication phases share the same link. Halving the bandwidth to 100100 Mbps leaves KstaleK_{\mathrm{stale}} in masked-step units at ∼23\sim 23, but doubles wall-clock cycle time.

Concurrent anchor cycles.

Running the anchor circuit at concurrency cc increases the delivered prior rate by c×c\times, at the cost of stretching individual prior staleness to c⋅Kstalec\cdot K_{\mathrm{stale}}. This trades fidelity for delivery rate.

Weaker DP compression.

Reducing PowerSGD from 64×64\times to 8×8\times, or shortening DiLoCo’s local horizon, increases the masked-step time and shrinks the PP-ratio term. Staleness KstaleK_{\mathrm{stale}} decreases, but only because the fast circuit slows down. Staleness must therefore be read together with throughput.

High-bandwidth (compute-bound) regime.

When links are fast enough that TmaskT_{\mathrm{mask}} is compute-bound, Tclean/TmaskT_{\mathrm{clean}}/T_{\mathrm{mask}} approaches 11. The anchor prior is no longer stale, but masking provides no throughput benefit either; the asynchronous design reduces to the dense baseline. Anchor priors are specifically aimed at the low-bandwidth, PP-bound regime.

H.6 Implications for design choices

The staleness analysis shapes two design choices in Section 3. First, the anchor momentum MtancM_{t}^{\mathrm{anc}} is updated with a slow EMA decay βanc\beta_{\mathrm{anc}} rather than replaced by each arriving anchor gradient: a single anchor gradient is stale by ∼20\sim 20 steps and noisy, but its principal directions remain informative when averaged over multiple cycles. Second, the spectral correction reweights the masked gradient toward anchor-supported eigendirections rather than substituting the anchor gradient for the masked one — since the anchor gradient is too stale to serve as a direct update signal, only its low-rank geometry is trustworthy at the ∼20\sim 20-step horizon.

Appendix I Training and Evaluation Datasets

This section details the training data, evaluation data, and shared training configuration used to produce the per-domain results in Table 1.

I.1 Training datasets

All training data is converted to a chat-message format (messages: [{user}, {assistant}]) with thinking disabled, then split 90/10 into train/validation unless the source provides a held-out split (GSM8K, Spider). Table 10 lists the source dataset and post-preprocessing row count per domain.

I.2 Evaluation datasets and metrics

Each domain run is evaluated on a fixed common suite plus one or more domain-specific tasks. The common suite consists of loglikelihood tasks (WinoGrande, PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge) and generative tasks (IFEval, GSM8K), all run via the in-training eval_callback. Domain-specific evaluations are summarized in Table 11; tasks marked lm-eval are run via the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024), and custom tasks are scored by dedicated scripts (Spider execution match, NarrativeQA token F1, QuALITY accuracy).

I.3 Shared training configuration

All baseline and masked runs share the configuration.

Model.

SmolLM3-Mid (1.2B parameters), BF16 weights and activations, FlashAttention 2, SmolLM3 chat template with thinking disabled.

Optimizer.

AdamW with (β1,β2)=(0.9, 0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,\,0.999). Peak learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, cosine schedule with min-LR ratio 0.10.1 and warmup ratio 0.030.03. Gradient norm clipped at 0.20.2.

Sequence handling.

Best-fit-decreasing packing enabled, except for short-context tasks (Spider, NarrativeQA, QuALITY) where packing is disabled. Maximum sequence length is task-dependent: 32,76832{,}768 for code/medical/science/commonsense/summarization/math, 2,0482{,}048 for SQL and NarrativeQA, 10,24010{,}240 for QuALITY, and 65,53665{,}536 for the general mixture. Loss is computed over assistant tokens only; Liger kernels are enabled.

Appendix J Squeezing Throughput from Data-Parallel Communication

Activation compression reduces the per-step cost of pipeline-parallel (PP) communication, but the throughput benefit is realized only if the data-parallel (DP) gradient all-reduce is reduced to a comparable level. Otherwise the DP all-reduce dominates wall-clock time and the activation savings are invisible. This section formalizes the trade-off, surveys the families of DP-compression techniques compatible with our setting, and identifies the operating points at which each becomes necessary.

J.1 Bottleneck analysis

Consider a model with NN parameters trained over KK-stage pipeline parallelism and DD-way data parallelism, with all communication crossing a network of bandwidth BB bytes/sec. Let SS denote the tokens per optimizer step, HH the hidden size, and bact,bgradb_{\mathrm{act}},b_{\mathrm{grad}} the bytes per activation and gradient element.

PP communication.

Pipeline parallelism transmits a forward activation and a backward gradient at each of the K−1K{-}1 boundaries. With activation compression ratio ρact∈(0,1]\rho_{\mathrm{act}}\in(0,1] (fraction of bytes still sent),

TPP=2​(K−1)​S​H​bact​ρactB.T_{\mathrm{PP}}=\frac{2\,(K{-}1)\,S\,H\,b_{\mathrm{act}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{act}}}{B}. (11)
DP communication.

A standard ring all-reduce of an N​bgradN\,b_{\mathrm{grad}}-byte gradient costs 2​(D−1)/D⋅N​bgrad2(D{-}1)/D\cdot N\,b_{\mathrm{grad}} bytes per rank (Patarasuk and Yuan, 2009). With per-step compression ratio ρDP\rho_{\mathrm{DP}} and outer-step interval τ\tau (one all-reduce per τ\tau optimizer steps, as in Local SGD or DiLoCo),

TDP=2​(D−1)/D⋅N​bgrad​ρDPB​τ.T_{\mathrm{DP}}=\frac{2\,(D{-}1)/D\cdot N\,b_{\mathrm{grad}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}}{B\,\tau}. (12)
Step time.

Under 1F1B-style scheduling, the per-step time is approximately max⁡(Tcompute,TPP,TDP)\max(T_{\mathrm{compute}},\,T_{\mathrm{PP}},\,T_{\mathrm{DP}}) when phases overlap, and their sum when they serialize. Throughput in tokens-per-second is TPS=S/step time\mathrm{TPS}=S/\text{step time}.

Concrete numbers.

For our reference configuration (N=1.2N{=}1.2B, H=2048H{=}2048, K=8K{=}8, D=8D{=}8, B=200B{=}200 Mbps ≈25\approx 25 MB/s, S=16,384S{=}16{,}384 tokens/step, BF16 throughout, A100 hardware), the components evaluate to:

  • •

    Compute (one optimizer step across all stages, with ∼50%\sim 50\% MFU): ∼100\sim 100 ms.

  • •

    PP communication at ρact=0.05\rho_{\mathrm{act}}=0.05 (95% masking): ∼1.9\sim 1.9 s, dominated by per-microbatch activation transfer at each of 77 boundaries in both directions.

  • •

    DP all-reduce uncompressed (ρDP=1\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}=1, τ=1\tau=1): ∼168\sim 168 s — nearly three minutes per step.

The uncompressed DP all-reduce alone is ∼90×\sim 90\times larger than the compressed PP transfer, and ∼1,700×\sim 1{,}700\times larger than the compute window. Activation compression on its own therefore yields no measurable speedup.

J.2 When DP compression is essential

For activation compression to translate into wall-clock speedup, TDPT_{\mathrm{DP}} must be reduced to within an order of magnitude of TPPT_{\mathrm{PP}}. From Eqs. (11)–(12), the required combined compression along the DP axis is

ρDPτ≲(K−1)​S​H​bact​ρact(D−1)/D⋅N​bgrad.\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}}{\tau}\;\lesssim\;\frac{(K{-}1)\,S\,H\,b_{\mathrm{act}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{act}}}{(D{-}1)/D\cdot N\,b_{\mathrm{grad}}}. (13)

For our configuration, this evaluates to roughly ρDP/τ≲1/100\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}/\tau\lesssim 1/100, so the joint per-step compression and frequency reduction must reach two orders of magnitude.

A single mechanism is rarely enough. Per-step gradient compressors above ∼32\sim 32–64×64\times tend to harm convergence, and outer-step intervals τ>500\tau>500 are at the edge of empirical stability for Local SGD / DiLoCo on language models. The practical strategies compose a compressor with a frequency-reduction technique — e.g., 64×64\times PowerSGD with τ=20\tau=20 DiLoCo — to multiply their effects.

J.3 Families of DP compression

DP-compression techniques fall into four orthogonal families. Methods within a family typically cannot be combined; methods across families typically can.

Quantization (F1).

Replace each gradient element with a low-bit representation. Examples include FP8/INT8, signSGD (Bernstein et al., 2018), and 1-bit Adam. Compression ranges from 2×2\times (FP16→\toFP8) to 32×32\times (1-bit). Stochastic rounding and error feedback (Karimireddy et al., 2019) are typically required at aggressive bit widths.

Sparsification (F2).

Transmit only the largest-magnitude entries. Top-KK sparsification (Lin et al., 2018) achieves 5050–100×100\times compression when paired with momentum correction and error feedback, but the indices themselves consume bandwidth and cap practical compression.

Low-rank factorization (F3).

Approximate the gradient matrix by a low-rank product. PowerSGD (Vogels et al., 2019) reaches 3232–256×256\times compression via rank-1 to rank-4 sketches with subspace iteration. The compressor is linear, so the projection commutes with all-reduce; error feedback recovers most of the lost precision.

Frequency reduction (F4).

Rather than compress each all-reduce, perform fewer of them. Local SGD (Stich, 2019) runs τ\tau inner SGD steps locally between all-reduces; DiLoCo (Douillard et al., 2023) adds an outer Nesterov optimizer and is empirically stable up to τ≈500\tau\approx 500 for LLM pretraining. Streaming DiLoCo (Douillard et al., 2025) pipelines the outer all-reduce with inner compute, removing the synchronous barrier.

Composition.

Frequency reduction multiplies with any per-step compressor. PowerSGD at ρDP=1/64\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}=1/64 combined with τ=20\tau=20 DiLoCo yields an effective 1280×1280\times reduction in DP bytes-per-step — enough to clear the threshold in Eq. (13) for our regime.

J.4 Comparison and selection

Table 12 summarizes the practical operating points.

The selection rule that follows from Eq. (13) is straightforward:

High bandwidth (≥1\geq 1 Gbps inter-node).

The required compression ratio is small, and PowerSGD at 3232–64×64\times alone usually meets it. No frequency reduction needed; implementation is intra-step with no algorithmic changes.

Low bandwidth (∼200\sim 200 Mbps).

Single-method compression tops out around 64×64\times without convergence loss, leaving roughly an order of magnitude on the table. Composition with DiLoCo (τ≥10\tau\geq 10) is required. Streaming DiLoCo additionally hides the outer all-reduce under inner compute, removing the synchronous barrier — this is our default configuration.

Federated or geo-distributed (≤50\leq 50 Mbps).

Composition is mandatory. Streaming DiLoCo with τ∈[50,500]\tau\in[50,500] stacked with ρDP≤1/64\rho_{\mathrm{DP}}\leq 1/64 is the only regime that delivers usable throughput; convergence quality must be re-validated at the chosen τ\tau.

Appendix K On the Compatibility with Dual-EMA Optimizers

A natural alternative to our spectral correction is to use the masked gradient as a noisy first-moment signal and reach for a dual-EMA optimizer that is known to tolerate gradient staleness, most notably AdEMAMix (Pagliardini et al., 2024). AdEMAMix replaces Adam’s single first-moment EMA with a mixture of a fast EMA m1m_{1} (β1≈0.9\beta_{1}\approx 0.9) and a slow EMA m2m_{2} (β3≈0.9999\beta_{3}\approx 0.9999). Its update rule is

θt+1=θt−η⋅m^1(t)+α​m2(t)v^(t)+ϵ,\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta\cdot\frac{\hat{m}_{1}^{(t)}+\alpha\,m_{2}^{(t)}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}^{(t)}}+\epsilon},

where m^1\hat{m}_{1} is bias-corrected, v^\hat{v} is Adam’s second moment, and α≈5\alpha\approx 5 controls the weight of the slow EMA. The empirical finding driving the design is that gradients can remain useful for tens of thousands of steps, and a single EMA cannot simultaneously weight the immediate past and the distant past.

This sounds superficially similar to our two-circuit design, both maintain a slow signal alongside a fast one, so it is reasonable to ask whether AdEMAMix could replace the spectral correction entirely, with the masked gradient serving as both inputs to the optimizer (the fast and slow EMAs would simply be two views of the same noisy signal). We argue this would not work in our setting, for two reasons.

(1) AdEMAMix mixes old gradients, not cleaner gradients.

The slow EMA m2m_{2} in AdEMAMix is an exponentially weighted average of the same gradients that feed the fast EMA. Its value comes from temporal smoothing of a noisy signal, not from any independent high-fidelity source. In our setting, the fast circuit’s gradients are biased away from the true gradient subspace by approximately ρ​σm2\rho\sigma_{m}^{2} even after spectral filtering (Lemma 2), and unbiased only in the sense of zero conditional mean. Smoothing TT such gradients with a slow EMA reduces the variance, but does not change the underlying noise spectrum: directions weakly supported by the signal remain weakly supported in the EMA. Our anchor circuit, by contrast, provides an independent signal computed from unmasked activations. Therefore, its principal subspace reflects the true gradient geometry, not a smoothed copy of the masked-gradient noise.

(2) Dual EMAs cannot recover lost subspaces.

A core claim of our analysis (Section E) is that the masked gradient is approximately isotropic relative to the anchor basis (Lemma 2, Assumption 6). This is why a low-rank spectral filter contracts noise quadratically in rank. AdEMAMix has no notion of an anchor basis; it operates entirely in the canonical parameter basis and applies the same dual-EMA dynamics elementwise. If the gradient signal lives in a low-rank subspace (as fine-tuning gradients do (Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022)) and the noise is approximately isotropic, AdEMAMix’s elementwise smoothing extracts the signal at rate O⁡(1/Teff)O(1/T_{\mathrm{eff}}) in noise variance, but discards the structural advantage of low-rankness. Our spectral filter exploits that structure directly.

However, we do not claim AdEMAMix is unhelpful in our setting. In fact, the two mechanisms are largely complementary. A natural composition is to apply AdEMAMix’s dual-EMA dynamics to the filtered gradient GtprojG_{t}^{\mathrm{proj}} rather than to the raw masked gradient. The fast EMA captures recent corrected directions, the slow EMA averages the filter’s output over many steps to further reduce residual noise, and the spectral correction continues to enforce subspace structure. We did not run this composition in the main experiments because our convergence analysis targets the single-EMA AdamW baseline directly. We believe this would be an interesting future direction to explore.
